text:
The debate, held at Lynn University in Boca Raton, Fla., was far more sedate than the candidates' clash a week earlier. The candidates sat at desks and interrupted each other only occasionally, in contrast to the aggressive confrontations that defined their last debate.

Mr. Obama, who has lost the lead he held until recently in many polls of the presidential race, struck a more combative stance throughout the debate.

Mr. Romney, while broadly critiquing Mr. Obama's leadership on foreign affairs, appeared to try to remain above the fray, often not engaging at all with the president's argument.

On a whole range of issues, including ending the war in Afghanistan, the possibility of U.S. military intervention in Syria and the use of drones as a tool of national-security policy, the two candidates were in broad agreement. They differed more sharply over how to tackle China's rise and thwart Iran's nuclear program, but in the main, the difference was mainly one of tone.

Repeatedly, the two men sought to turn their conversation to domestic policy, roaming across issues including the federal bailout of the U.S. auto industry and the deficit, a last bid to directly address millions of voters on the presidential campaign's core topics.

Mr. Romney broadly criticized Mr. Obama's leadership on foreign affairs, saying the president began his first term with "an apology tour" through the Middle East. And the Republican nominee pushed back at Mr. Obama's criticism that his stance on foreign affairs has been inconsistent.

"Attacking me is not an agenda," Mr. Romney said. "Attacking me is not talking about how we're going to deal with the challenges that exist in the Middle East and take advantage of the opportunity there and stem the tide of this violence."

Mr. Obama said that what the country needs is "strong, steady leadership, not wrong and reckless leadership all over the map." He called the notion that he has apologized for America "probably the biggest whopper that's been told during the course of this campaign."

The approaches taken by both candidates made it harder than the first two debates to see where the advantage lay.

Sen. Rob Portman (R., Ohio), who took on the role of Mr. Obama in Mr. Romney's preparations for the debates, said the Republican candidate "appeared more presidential."

"It was almost like he was the incumbent, and President Obama was the challenger who was behind and on the attack," he said.

Senior White House adviser David Plouffe, who was Mr. Obama's 2008 campaign manager, said, "We would win this race if it were held today. This is a debate about strength and who's going to be commander in chief. So if you can't sit there and take that from your political opponent, how are you going to deal with the people who want to do America harm?"

The candidates' most pointed foreign-policy exchanges, stylistically at least, came during a discussion of how to handle Iran's nuclear program and the U.S. relationship with Israel.

The two drew slightly different "red lines" on when to intervene in Iran militarily.

Mr. Romney stuck with his position that Iran "must not develop nuclear capability." Mr. Obama says he will stop Iran from obtaining a weapon, but his campaign has said Mr. Romney's red line is more likely to trigger military intervention sooner.

Mr. Romney said he would take a harder line than has Mr. Obama on sanctions by trying to close loopholes, further isolate Tehran diplomatically and indict Iran's president for inciting "genocide." He suggested the Obama administration's early attempts to increase negotiations with Tehran were a mistake. "It is essential for a president to show strength from the very beginning," he said.

Mr. Obama said he had marshaled international agreements for the toughest sanctions against Iran that had ever been put in place. He said the U.S. would "stand with Israel if they are attacked" and promised: "As long as I'm president of the United States, Iran will not get a nuclear weapon."

Throughout the debate Mr. Romney appeared to temper some of the tough stances he has taken on foreign-policy issues during the campaign.

He passed up an opportunity at the start of the debate to continue his pointed criticism of Mr. Obama's handling of the attack last month on a U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya, that killed four Americans, including the U.S. ambassador. Instead, Mr. Romney, who has repeatedly raised questions about Libya on the campaign trail, talked more broadly about tackling the challenges in the Middle East.

"I congratulate him on taking out Osama bin Laden and going after the leadership in al Qaeda. But we can't kill our way out of this mess," Mr. Romney said.

Mr. Romney was also cautious when detailing a role for the U.S. military, saying: "We don't want another Iraq. We don't want another Afghanistan." With the remark Mr. Romney distanced himself from the Republican president who oversaw the start of those wars, George W. Bush. "That's not the right course for us," Mr. Romney said.

Mr. Obama argued that Mr. Romney was more hawkish than he was portraying himself, an argument similar to the one the president has made in recent days about Mr. Romney's more centrist tone on social and domestic issues. The president also mocked his opponent's views as naive, such as his approach to Russia. "The 1980s are now calling to ask for their foreign policy back," Mr. Obama said.

Messrs. Obama and Romney repeatedly steered the discussion back to the economic issues that voters tend to regard as more important.

Mr. Obama said the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan took resources away from domestic concerns and that winding down both of those conflicts would allow the government to focus on needs at home.

Mr. Romney argued that promoting "principles of peace" abroad "begins with a strong economy here at home." He cited the U.S. debt as a national security threat, saying, "We have weakened our economy. We need a strong economy."

Mr. Obama, discussing scheduled cuts to spending on the military and other government programs, said "It will not happen," possibly his most definitive comment on the matter. The cuts are set to take place Dec. 31 as part of last year's deal to raise the U.S.'s borrowing limit.

The candidates also played to voters in the industrial Midwest by presenting themselves as tough on China.

The debate, moderated by Bob Schieffer of CBS News, came at a critical moment for both campaigns, marking one of the last chances the candidates would have to change the course of the race.

Mr. Obama is in his most vulnerable position all year, with a new Wall Street Journal/NBC News poll showing he has dropped below the critical 50% threshold among likely voters. His support among women voters -- a critical constituency -- has softened in recent weeks, and several polls show he is virtually tied with Mr. Romney in battleground states that will decide the election.

(See related article: "Rivals Seek Points By Going Off-Topic" -- WSJ October 23, 2012)
title: Rivals Duel in Final Face-Off --- Obama Calls Romney 'Reckless'; Romney Seeks Stronger Global Role for U.S.

text:
The president is expected to face a renewed challenge from Beijing over continued U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, say administration officials and foreign-policy specialists. And many Asian officials fear the dispute between Japan and China over an atoll in the East China Sea could escalate further and force Washington -- Tokyo's treaty ally -- into a larger role.

The Obama administration over the past year has been touting its intention to tilt Washington's strategic focus away from the Middle East and toward Asia, because of the region's economic growth and China's increasing power. And Republican challenger Mitt Romney had campaigned on expanding U.S. Navy capabilities to contain China.

But few regional analysts believe Mr. Obama will be able to significantly shift U.S. focus away from the Mideast over the next four years. Just weeks after his re-election, for example, he must decide whether to approve U.S. participation in a fourth round of negotiations this year with Iran over its nuclear program.

Israeli officials now say military action could be needed by next summer to prevent Iran from reaching the capability for making atomic weapons. Iran insists its nuclear program is purely for civilian purposes.

The impact of Western sanctions has increased, contributing to a 40% fall recently in the value of Iran's currency. The pressure is raising expectations that Tehran might be forced to compromise.

"On Iran, there does seem to be some traction toward a new direction," said Rob Malley, who oversees Mideast issues for the International Crisis Group, a global analysis and advocacy organization.

But the White House will need to decide if Iranian concessions will satisfy Israel and the U.S.'s Arab allies, as well as pro-Israel lawmakers on Capitol Hill.

Elsewhere, pressure on the U.S. is mounting to support international military action in Syria and Mali. Sectarian conflict in Syria has intensified, with human rights groups reporting nearly 40,000 killed over the past 18 months. Arab officials fear the conflict is more rapidly spilling across borders, risking unrest in Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq and Turkey.

During the campaign, Messrs. Obama and Romney campaigned against directly sending U.S. troops into Syria. But the Republican candidate said he would ensure that more arms reach rebels fighting President Bashar al-Assad's rule, while Mr. Obama said he supports more nonlethal assistance.

In North Africa, the U.S. and Europe are supporting African-led military action in Mali, where al Qaeda and other extremist groups have secured safe-havens this year.

The Obama administration has been forced to more aggressively intervene in the conflict following the September attack on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya. U.S. intelligence officials believe members of al Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, the extremist group's North African affiliate, may have helped plan the attack, which killed four Americans, including Ambassador Christopher Stevens.

A wild card for Mr. Obama's second term will be the Arab-Israeli conflict, said Mideast analysts.

Peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians have been frozen for nearly two years, following Mr. Obama's aggressive early initiatives aimed at forging an agreement.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has refused to return to talks until Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu freezes all Jewish construction in disputed areas. The Israeli leader, objecting to that demand, has said the Palestinians are seeking to set preconditions for any talks.

In recent weeks, however, Mr. Abbas has said he would seek a vote at the United Nations General Assembly that would recognize Palestine as an independent state. A positive vote would have limited legal effect, as only the U.N. Security Council can grant such status. But Mr. Abbas' initiative could rekindle regional tensions, Mideast analysts said, and potentially lead to the U.S. Congress cutting aid for the Palestinian Authority.

Mr. Obama also will come under pressure to more directly engage Latin America, with Mexico and Brazil emerging as among the most important U.S. trading partners. The threats posed to U.S. borders by narco-trafficking gangs in Mexico could eclipse those posed by Mideast-based terrorist groups, national-security experts believe.

text:
(WSJ March 31, 2012)

(END)

Mitt Romney's labeling of Russia this week as America's "No. 1 geopolitical foe" has drawn attention to his emerging hawkishness on several foreign policy fronts, from China's monetary policy to the war in Afghanistan -- a trend that contrasts to his more muted style on domestic issues.

The Russia remark has fanned concerns among both Romney supporters and nonpartisan foreign-policy experts that Mr. Romney's desire to contrast himself with President Barack Obama has led the GOP candidate to take positions that would be difficult to maintain if he wins the presidency.

"I think Obama's foreign policy is seriously flawed, but I worry that too much of Romney's criticism is driven by what he thinks is best politically, and not by any larger strategic vision," said Dimitri Simes, a Russia expert who was a Romney foreign-policy adviser in 2008.

Mr. Romney's Russia blast came after Mr. Obama was heard on an open microphone in South Korea this week promising Russia's president more "flexibility" on arms-defense talks after the November election. Those comments drew widespread condemnation from Republicans, including House Speaker John Boehner, who wrote to Mr. Obama asking him to "clarify" what he meant.

Mr. Romney went further, saying on CNN he found it "terribly wrong" that the president would offer any assurances to a country he described as "one of the world's worst actors."

Some Romney aides concede the former governor's portrayal of Russia was overstated. But Rich Williamson, a former aide to President Ronald Reagan and current Romney foreign-policy adviser, defended the thrust of his foreign-policy remarks. "Campaigns are about presenting views and drawing contrasts," Mr. Williamson said. "Mitt Romney has laid out his detailed positions already, and now he is drawing contrasts."

Others say they see a different pattern. "Romney keeps staking out positions that are meant to be sharply at odds with Obama, but also happen to be at odds with what he would have to do if he were president," said Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East adviser to five secretaries of state going back to the Reagan administration.

In several cases, Mr. Romney has cut against the views of his top advisers. One of his veteran foreign-policy hands, former George W. Bush official Mitchell Reiss, spoke approvingly of Obama administration outreach to the Taliban in January. Sen. John McCain, one of Mr. Romney's top supporters, also supports talks with the former Afghan leaders who were ousted by the U.S. after Sept. 11, 2001.

Asked about potential negotiations with the Taliban in a debate soon after, Mr. Romney shot back: "We should not negotiate with the Taliban. We should defeat the Taliban."

Mr. Romney has been critical of Obama policies toward China, accusing Mr. Obama of being a "near supplicant to Beijing." He has promised to impose sanctions on China over its currency policies on his first day in office.

But Robert Kagan, another of Mr. Romney's top foreign-policy aides, has singled out Mr. Obama's diplomacy in Asia as one of the White House's chief foreign-policy accomplishments. Two of Mr. Romney's top economic advisers, Glenn Hubbard and Greg Mankiw, have also urged a softer line toward China on its currency.

Over the course of a campaign that has mainly skirted foreign-policy issues, Mr. Romney has backed remaining in Afghanistan until the U.S. can claim victory there. He has promised to boost military spending and to increase the size of the Navy. He has accused Mr. Obama of failing to stand up to Iran's nuclear threat and undermining U.S. ties to Israel.

The core of his argument is that he would restore the nation to world leadership and protect its exceptional role in international affairs, which he says have dissipated under Mr. Obama.

Mr. Obama's supporters point to strikes on al Qaeda leaders, including Osama bin Laden, and the use of diplomatic and other tools to pressure Iran and topple Libya's dictator, as evidence of a muscular foreign policy.

Mr. Romney's foreign-policy persona in 2008 was in some ways softer and more nuanced than it is now. He was similarly hawkish toward Iran, and vowed four years ago to double the size of the Guantanamo prison in Cuba. But he also spoke about the need to buttress U.S. diplomacy and regional cooperation. To combat Islamic radicalism, he proposed a multinational summit, which he called a Partnership for Prosperity and Progress.

As they eye a general election, Romney advisers complain that the primaries have provided few openings for Mr. Romney to step out on the foreign-policy front, despite what they insist are deep differences between his views and those of Mr. Obama. "But as we move toward the general election, you will hear him talking a lot more about his views of the U.S. and its future in the world," Mr. Kagan said.
