text:
Above all, Mr. Obama has presented himself as the antidote to the Bush Administration and all he said it represented: costly wars, harsh interrogations, global opprobrium. Mr. Romney should expect the President to try to define him as a Bush retread, and to paint America's foreign policy options as a choice between sober restraint and swaggering bellicosity.


We don't expect Mr. Romney to offer an explicit defense of the Bush Doctrine, never mind that its core tenets -- keeping weapons of mass destruction out of the hands of rogue regimes and promoting liberal democracy in places like Egypt -- are ones Mr. Obama rhetorically endorses. Nor do we anticipate that Mr. Romney will retreat from the protectionist rhetoric he's been peddling on China, though it would be nice to hear him recognize that the biggest "currency manipulator" in the world today is the U.S. Federal Reserve.

But Mr. Romney can help himself by offering a serious critique of Mr. Obama's foreign policy that doesn't descend to cliches (e.g., "I won't ever apologize for America"), and by laying out a vision that answers the needs of both the national interest and the self-interest of everyday Americans.

Mr. Romney should also give full credit where it's due, not least because some graciousness would be a refreshing contrast to Mr. Obama's abrasive partisanship in an area where Americans yearn for consensus. That means not only commending the President for the bin Laden raid, but also for the areas in which the Administration has adopted the policies of its predecessor: the reauthorization of the Patriot Act; the use of military tribunals; the intensification of drone strikes; the (admittedly reluctant) non-closure of Guantanamo. All that should cause some indigestion among Mr. Obama's friends at MSNBC.

Mr. Romney can also play to his own strengths by pointing out that a U.S. economic revival is crucial to world stability. One reason America has less sway now than it did when Mr. Obama took office is that the world won't heed a great power whose policies produce slow growth and runaway debt.

Ronald Reagan understood that before he could defeat the Soviet Union he had to show again the superiority of the American model of economic freedom. The U.S. military will inexorably and rapidly shrink without growth of 3% or more. This theme is right in Mr. Romney's wheelhouse.


Moving to the President's record, he likes to boast about responsibly ending the war in Iraq. Yet the war had already been won when Mr. Obama became President thanks to a surge that he opposed as a Senator -- even as he later tried to emulate it in Afghanistan under the same military commander. Mr. Obama also tried to negotiate a Status of Forces Agreement with Iraq that would have maintained a residual U.S. military presence in the country, and Joe Biden even offered to "bet you my Vice Presidency" on the negotiations succeeding. But they pursued it too half-heartedly to entice the Iraqis to a deal.

The result is that American soldiers won a victory in Iraq at great cost only so Mr. Obama could squander the strategic fruits of their victory: a viable alliance with Baghdad and a bulwark against Tehran. Mr. Obama may think that he's come out of this as a political winner, but nobody is happier about his Iraq policy than the mullahs in Iran.

Now the U.S. runs similar risks in Afghanistan, the war Mr. Obama once said was the one we must win but from which his Vice President last week promised full withdrawal by 2014 -- let the Taliban do what it may. Given that Mr. Obama signed a Status of Forces Agreement with the Afghan government in May that explicitly opens the door to a post-2014 U.S. military presence, Mr. Romney might ask whether the President stands by his own signature -- or by his Vice President? It can't be both.

Mr. Obama will no doubt reply that the U.S. cannot endlessly be at war in the Middle East. That's true, but Mr. Obama's policies of premature military withdrawals have increased rather than diminished the chances that we will be at war in the Middle East again. The Administration can hope that its training of Afghan forces will suffice to keep the country together after 2014. But if it doesn't and the Taliban return, we will find ourselves back at square one -- 2,000 lives and hundreds of billions of dollars later.


Mr. Obama is also courting war in the Middle East by his ambivalent posture on Iran's nuclear designs. Mr. Romney can applaud Mr. Obama for insisting that "all options are on the table" when it comes to thwarting those designs, and for publicly opposing a containment strategy for a nuclear Iran.

Yet the Obama Administration has consistently undermined its own message by advertising that it believes a military option would be ineffectual, by failing to provide Israel with reassurances that it needn't consider its own military options, and by first resisting sanctions until Congress passed them and then handing out waivers to those same sanctions. The result is that Iran has not been remotely deterred despite sanctions, and it is now only months away from being able to produce weapons-grade uranium.

If Mr. Obama implies (as he no doubt will) that Mr. Romney wants to start a third Middle Eastern war, the answer is that the only way to prevent one is to let Tehran know we're deadly serious. Weakness and indecision invite war, while credibility and resolve still have a chance to prevent it.

The same mixed-messaging helps explain why America's position throughout the rest of the Middle East is dramatically weaker than it was four years ago. The President's Cairo speech promised a new beginning with the Muslim world. Yet in practice Mr. Obama was friendlier to Hosni Mubarak than George W. Bush had been until Mr. Obama cut him loose in the final days, and he made no effort to push the Arab autocracies toward reform before their downfall.

The result, if you can believe it, is the worst of both worlds. The U.S. has become even less popular with the publics of such countries as Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan and Lebanon than it was in the last year of Mr. Bush's Presidency. And it also has less credibility with the rulers of those countries that have been our allies. When the Saudis invaded Bahrain, they never bothered to tell the U.S.

So much, then, for the transformative powers of Mr. Obama's charisma and good intentions -- which have also failed to work their supposed wonders on the likes of Russia's Vladimir Putin (who continues to obstruct us at the U.N.), or of China's new leadership (which is trying to lay claim to most of the South China Sea), or even of little Cuba, which continues to hold American Alan Gross as a hostage. It has occurred too late to the President and his advisers that "smart diplomacy" mainly entails the calibrated uses of power, not the promiscuous promotion of personality.

As for Mr. Romney, he can't and shouldn't promise to return the genies to their bottles by reversing the gains of Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood or renegotiating a new military agreement with Iraq. He also seems disinclined to propose anything more than Mr. Obama is doing to depose the Assad regime in Syria. But if nothing else he can explain the risks that Syria's expanding war poses to U.S. interests and allies and how a defeat for Assad would mean a defeat for Iran's growing regional influence.


More broadly, Mr. Romney can promise to restore America's credibility as a guarantor of peace and stability -- not simply for the sake of far-flung peoples and countries, but for our own.

America has been the chief underwriter of global order for nearly seven decades, which has required large defense budgets and difficult military commitments. But we have also been a major beneficiary: no world wars; open sea lanes; expanding trade and freedom; and the human and economic possibilities of a world that, until Mr. Obama came to office, was freer than it had ever previously been.

In his farewell interviews, Mr. Obama's first Defense Secretary, Robert Gates, made a point of quoting Reagan's line that he had lived through many wars but not one of them began because the U.S. was too strong. Mr. Obama's first term has been marked by economic decline at home and less respect and influence abroad. Four more years of the same will tempt the world's rogues to become even more assertive.

On Monday night Mr. Romney can make clear that his foreign policy will understand that strength at home and confidence abroad aren't incompatible objectives, but are mutually reinforcing.
title: The Foreign Policy Debate

text:
Mr. Santorum believes the United States must lead the struggle for freedom throughout the world, on grounds of morality and national security, which he believes go hand in hand. He does not like the drift away from leadership and engagement in that struggle, especially under President Obama. He often quotes Lech Walesa's recent lament: "The United States was always the last resort and hope for all other nations," Poland's first post-communist president said. "There was the hope, whenever something was going wrong, one could count on the United States. Today, we have lost that hope."

Mr. Santorum wants to restore the hope that America will rescue those for whom things have gone terribly wrong. In Congress, he supported aid programs to help Africans suffering from AIDS and other terrible diseases (laying the foundation for his friendship with U2 singer Bono). He also has sponsored legislation to support democratic opponents of the Syrian and Iranian tyrannies -- because their leaders, the Assad dynasty in Syria and Iran's Ali Khamenei and Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, threaten American and Israeli security, and because he wants to support moderate Muslims living under such regimes.

After leaving the Senate in 2007, Mr. Santorum wrote about foreign policy frequently for the Ethics and Public Policy Center, where he was a fellow until June of 2011. In essays written for the center, he acknowledges that terrorists are indeed inspired by radical Islam -- but he wants to work with Muslims who do not wage jihad, subjugate women or oppress minorities. He's specific about the radicals: They are evil men who have perverted the meaning of "martyrdom," changing it from the act of dying for one's faith to killing others to advance the dominion of one's faith.

His opposition to tyranny abroad has been a constant in his political career. Even in the final days of his losing 2006 re-election campaign, Mr. Santorum never stopped calling for action against Iran and Syria. Apparently, Pennsylvanians weren't impressed by his Iran Freedom and Support Act, enacted in 2006, which imposed sanctions on the regime and authorized $100 million annually for the democratic opposition, or his 2003 Syria Accountability Act.

But today he looks prescient and gutsy. Back then, the Bush administration was trying to run away from such ideas. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice at one point turned to a Democrat, then-Sen. Joe Biden, to block Mr. Santorum's Iran bill, before it finally passed. But Mr. Santorum's basic vision has prevailed.

He foresaw that we would eventually have to confront the Iranian and Syrian regimes, and he was one of the first to point out the intercontinental anti-American alliance involving Iran, Syria, Russia, China, Venezuela, Bolivia, Cuba, Honduras and Nicaragua. He calls this a "gathering storm," as members of the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps enter our hemisphere through the Venezuelan capital of Caracas, accompanied by military equipment and components.

He is right to be concerned. Former supporters of the Hugo Chavez regime in Venezuela, worried at the direction of events in their country, have told American officials that there are Iranian missiles in Venezuela capable of hitting the U.S. More obvious are the Shiite mosques suddenly popping up in Venezuela and its near neighborhood.

If we keep leading from "behind," as the president puts it, the lowest common denominator of Western resolve will define our policy. That's disastrous for people in other countries who are standing up to tyranny, and it emboldens America's enemies like Iran or the Taliban. Mr. Santorum believes things would be different if we were committed to defeating those enemies, and he is convinced that the region and the world would be far safer if there were regime change in Damascus and Tehran.

That's why he has long called for support for the Iranian opposition and favors arming and training the Free Syrian Army to bring down the Assad regime. He advocates zeroing in on the foreign scientists -- from Russia, for instance -- who work on the mullahs' nuclear-bomb program and declaring them enemy combatants.

Mr. Santorum hopes that American financial and moral support for the Iranian opposition will catalyze the simmering democratic revolution there, which in turn would likely tilt the balance of power in Syria once the regime in Tehran was no longer there to support Damascus. If that strategy fails, he said in Florida in January, he would go with the military option against Iran's nuclear weapons project, in close cooperation with Israel.

Unlike President Obama, Mr. Santorum believes that an explicit linkage of American and Israeli military and intelligence assets would greatly increase chances of success. And since we'd be blamed for any unilateral Israeli strike, he sees no point in separating from the Israelis on this most crucial issue.

Beyond the Middle East, Mr. Santorum believes that we should fully develop our missile-defense system -- reversing Mr. Obama's abrupt cancellation or limitation of the systems destined for our Czech and Polish NATO allies. He supports the development of measures to protect our satellites and other facilities against electromagnetic-pulse weapons. He has written that if elected, he would reverse many of the Obama defense cuts.

Above all, the world would know that a President Santorum would be determined to revive the hope that Poland's Lech Walesa declares lost -- the hope that America would be the last line of defense for freedom and virtue. Just as Grandpa Pietro taught.


Mr. Ledeen, a scholar at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, is the author of "Virgil's Golden Egg and Other Neapolitan Miracles" (Transaction, 2011).
title: Santorum Was Right About Iran -- When It Was Unpopular

text:
In that speech and other comments by the presumptive Republican nominee and his advisers, the Romney camp spent the day carefully sketching out a stance that is more assertive than the Obama administration's.

Mr. Romney's visit to Israel comes midway through an international swing that includes stops in London and Poland. The trip is designed largely to showcase Mr. Romney on an international stage, in part to counter polls that consistently show national-security to be an area of relative strength for President Barack Obama in a tight presidential campaign.

The GOP hopeful has tried to walk a careful line, drawing implicit contrasts with Obama policies without being openly critical of the president while on foreign soil. But the Romney call for a harsher stance on Iran, like a similar pledge to be tougher in penalizing China for its economic policies, is one of the most prominent areas of divergence in a campaign largely dominated by domestic issues.

Mr. Romney stopped short of actually endorsing an Israeli military strike, and his campaign didn't say whether a Romney administration would provide direct assistance for such a mission. But unlike the Obama administration, Mr. Romney didn't discourage Israel from considering a military option or waiting before doing so.

Dan Senor, a senior foreign-policy adviser to Mr. Romney, was more explicit, telling reporters that "if Israel has to take action on its own in order to stop Iran from developing that capability, the governor would respect that decision." Asked about that comment in a later interview with ABC News, Mr. Romney said: "I respect the right of Israel to defend itself and America always on the side of Israel but I'm not going to be more specific than that with regards to the actions Israel might take."

The words suggest a Romney administration would be more open to Israeli military action than the Obama administration has been. Mr. Obama also has repeatedly said that Israel has the right to defend itself, but the administration, publicly and privately, has been trying to dissuade Israel from considering an attack now so economic sanctions -- ramped up this summer to include a European ban on Iranian oil purchases -- can be given time to work.

Defense Secretary Leon Panetta, who began a five-day Middle East trip that includes Israel this week, wouldn't be drawn into the debate. But he echoed the Republican candidate's underlying sentiment, saying the U.S. respects Israel's right to make its own security decisions.

"We respect their sovereignty and their ability to make decisions with regards to their own security," Mr. Panetta said en route to Tunis. At the same time, he said economic sanctions against Iran are having a "significant impact" on the country's economy and will do so even more in the coming weeks. He said the international effort "has been effective in making clear to Iran that they can't continue to do what they're doing."

The position Mr. Romney sketched out is consistent with the critique his advisers have offered of Obama policy toward Iran -- that it is flawed because it lacks a real military threat to back up economic sanctions.

Mr. Romney's warnings on Iran's nuclear capability came after a day of meetings with Israeli officials here in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called existing Iran sanctions ineffective. "We have to be honest and say that all the sanctions and diplomacy so far have not set back the Iranian program by one iota," Mr. Netanyahu said.

In his speech, Mr. Romney said "it is our fervent hope that diplomatic and economic measures will" dissuade Iran. But he also defended those who want to take a firmer stand. "It is sometimes said that those who are the most committed to stopping the Iranian regime from securing nuclear weapons are reckless and provocative and inviting war," he said, taking a jab at the president who once warned that too much "loose talk" about a war with Iran is counterproductive.

"The opposite is true. We are the true peacemakers," Mr. Romney said.

Many Israeli officials would prefer that, if there is military action to set back Iran's nuclear program, it be launched by the U.S., which has a larger and more powerful array of weapons to bring to the task.

If Israel were to move on its own, though, it would like more than just rhetorical support from the U.S. Israel might seek more and larger American-made bunker-busting bombs, as well as more access to American satellite-produced intelligence. Israel also would like more U.S. help in refueling its bombers on the long flight to Iran. It has ordered new U.S.-made transport planes that could be used for that purpose, but deliveries aren't due to start until next year.

Obama administration officials point out that, despite tensions between Mr. Obama and Mr. Netanyahu, military cooperation between the U.S. and Israel has stepped up in multiple ways in recent months. He has increased funding for Israel's missile-defense program, provided some advanced bombs and opened the way to increased coordination on military exercises.

Mr. Romney has deemed those moves inadequate and vowed to employ even harsher sanctions on Iran and eliminate exemptions for countries such as China. He has also promised to station an aircraft carrier task force in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Persian Gulf region.

"This is where Romney, I think, who is rather stiff and awkward on the campaign trail, sees an advantage," said Aaron Miller, a public policy fellow at the Woodrow Wilson Center and a former State Department official.

Mr. Netanyahu invited Mr. Romney and his wife, Ann, to his home for a private dinner and lauded the former Massachusetts governor, who worked with him at the Boston Consulting Group briefly after both men finished business school.

"We've known each other for many decades, since you were a young man," Mr. Netanyahu told Mr. Romney. "You've been a personal friend of mine and a strong friend of the state of Israel."

Mr. Romney spent much of the day in meetings with officials, but on Monday he is scheduled to be at a fundraiser, where U.S. citizens -- including casino owner Sheldon Adelson and New York Jets owner Woody Johnson -- will pay at least $50,000 to attend.


Adam Entous and Joshua Mitnick contributed to this article.
title: Election 2012: Romney Talks Tough --- He Defends Israel's Right to Prevent Iran Nuclear Weapon

text:
At home, a shooting in January killed six and wounded U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords and others. In May, U.S. forces raided a compound in Pakistan and killed al Qaeda head Osama bin Laden after a long hunt. Summer was filled with partisan bickering over the typically procedural matter of raising the debt ceiling, with an 11th-hour vote averting default but costing the U.S. one of its triple-A ratings. And the autumn boiled over with the loosely affiliated protest movement Occupy Wall Street expressing popular discontent across the U.S.

Through it all, the world said goodbye and good riddance to leaders reviled by many -- Egypt's Hosni Mubarak, Tunisia's Zine el-Abidine ben Ali, bin Laden, Libya's Moammar Gadhafi and North Korea's Kim Jong Il. Others were close to leaving as the year ended.

Here is a summary of news events from The Wall Street Journal. In most cases, the dates reflect when the items were published, not the date of the event.

JANUARY

4 Mark Zuckerberg's Facebook raised $500 million from Goldman Sachs and others, in a high-profile private offering. Goldman later had to amend the offering, which raised $1.5 billion all told and valued the company at $50 billion, to avoid running afoul of U.S. securities rules concerning private ownership.

Republican Rep. John Boehner took over as House speaker.

8 On this day, Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, an Arizona Democrat, was shot in the head as she spoke with constituents outside a supermarket near Tucson. Six others were killed in the attack. Jared Loughner was later charged with murder and dozens of other counts.

12 China has launched trading in the yuan in the U.S. for the first time, an explicit endorsement of the fast-growing market in the currency.

15 Pope Benedict attributed a miracle to John Paul II, advancing the case to have his predecessor declared a saint in record time.

18 Tunisian politicians formed a caretaker government. The new cabinet, which will run affairs until new elections are held, followed the overthrow of longtime President Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali -- the first leader in the broader Mideast felled by a popular uprising in nearly two decades.

Steve Jobs is taking an unexpected leave from running Apple.

20 The GOP-led House voted 245-189 to repeal the health-care law. The Senate didn't take up the measure.

21 Federal agents conducted a record mob sweep. Morning raids in New York, New Jersey and Rhode Island netted 119 people. In all, 127 people were charged with crimes including fraud, loan-sharking and murder.

Google co-founder Larry Page was tapped to take the reins as chief executive from Eric Schmidt in a surprise change atop the Internet giant.

26 Thousands of protesters clashed with police in Egypt. The demonstrators called for the ouster of President Hosni Mubarak, an end to Egypt's emergency law and an increase in the minimum wage. In the days, weeks and months to follow, popular unrest would spread across the region.

28 Hedge-fund manager John Paulson personally netted over $5 billion in profits in 2010, likely the largest one-year haul in investing history.

31 Syria's president said he will push for political change. Bashar al-Assad acknowledged that Arab rulers would need to do more to accommodate their people's aspirations amid the unrest in Egypt, Tunisia and Yemen.

FEBRUARY

1 A U.S. judge ruled the health overhaul is unconstitutional because it requires Americans to buy insurance, in a blow to the law. Weeks later, another judge upheld the law.

4 A whistleblower group says in a lawsuit that Bank of New York Mellon currency traders created fake trades and overcharged Virginia pension funds by at least $20 million.

6 On this day, the Green Bay Packers win Super Bowl XLV over the Pittsburgh Steelers, 31-25.

8 J.P. Morgan planned to accept gold as collateral in some transactions, adding to a movement that places the metal in the top tier of asset classes.

9 On this day, plans emerged for Germany's Deutsche Borse to acquire NYSE Euronext, operator of the New York Stock Exchange. The deal would later face resistance as European regulators expressed competition concerns.

11 On this day, Egypt's Mubarak stepped down as leader of the Arab world's most-populous country, handing power to the military. At least 846 Egyptians were killed during 18 days of protests that ousted him, a fact-finding committee later said.

14 China passed Japan in 2010 to become the world's second-largest economy, after the U.S.

15 President Obama unveiled a $3.73 trillion budget that would close or reduce 200 federal programs but make only a modest dent in long-term deficits.

16 A funeral in Bahrain swelled into growing clashes with security forces, in the first Mideast unrest to pit a Shiite majority against Sunni rulers.

17 Borders filed for bankruptcy protection. The bookstore chain later entered liquidation.

23 Col. Moammar Gadhafi vowed to fight on as a rebellion that had been creeping for days swept across Libya. The unrest threw Libya's oil industry into turmoil as ports closed and foreign companies suspended operations.

24 The Obama administration, in a reversal, said it believed a law defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman violated the Constitution.

25 The death toll reached at least 110 from an earthquake that devastated Christchurch, New Zealand. The year closed with strong aftershocks.

MARCH

4 President Obama said publicly for the first time that Gadhafi must give up power. Later in the month, the U.S. helped lead creation of an air shield over Libya that eventually came under NATO auspices.

5 The U.S. jobless rate fell below 9% for the first time in nearly two years.

8 Charlie Sheen was fired from the Warner Bros. sitcom "Two and a Half Men" amid controversy over alleged drug use and inflammatory statements.

Subway surpassed McDonald's as the world's largest restaurant chain, measured by number of outlets.

10 Illinois Gov. Quinn signed a bill abolishing the death penalty, making his the 16th state to end capital punishment.

11 On this day, Japan was struck by the most-powerful earthquake to hit the country on record, triggering a devastating tsunami. Thousands were killed and billions of dollars in damages resulted. A nuclear crisis later developed at a stricken plant. Three days later, in the first trading session since the disaster, Japanese stocks slid 4.4%.

15 Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway will pay $9 billion for chemical maker Lubrizol, the investor's latest foray into the industrial sector. At the end of the month, David Sokol, a leading contender to succeed Buffett, resigned amid revelations about trading stock in Lubrizol.

17 Data showed U.S. sales of Diet Coke overtook those of Pepsi-Cola for the first time in 2010.

18 G-7 nations banded together to stem a rise in the value of the Japanese yen, the first time they have joined to intervene in currency markets since 2000.

19 AT&T reached a deal to acquire T-Mobile USA from Deutsche Telekom for $39 billion, a combination that would create the nation's largest wireless carrier. But the proposed tie-up buckled later in the year amid competition concerns from the Justice Department and was abandoned.

22 Citigroup will reinstate its dividend at a penny per share after a reverse stock split to cut its shares outstanding to 2.9 billion from 29 billion.

23 Died: Elizabeth Taylor, 79, the violet-eyed actress who enchanted movie audiences -- and a string of husbands.

26 Died: Geraldine Ferraro, 75, the first woman to appear on the presidential ballot.

31 A departing federal bailout official told a House panel that firms deemed "too big to fail" remain a threat to the economy in TARP's wake.

A Russian investor paid $100 million for a Silicon Valley mansion, the highest known price paid for a single-family home in the U.S.

APRIL

2 Nasdaq OMX and IntercontinentalExchange announced a $11.3 billion offer aimed at sinking a deal for the New York Stock Exchange's parent company to be bought by Deutsche Boerse. The duo went hostile before the Justice Department nixed the deal on monopoly grounds.

5 The White House said the alleged 9/11 plotters will face military trials at Guantanamo, scrapping its effort to try them in civilian courts.

7 Portugal said it would ask the EU for a financial bailout, becoming the third nation in the 17-member euro zone to turn to its peers for help.

8 Europe's central bank became the first monetary authority in a major developed economy to raise interest rates since the global financial crisis struck. The ECB increased its benchmark by a quarter point to 1.25%.

12 Japan boosted its nuclear-accident severity rating to a 7, which indicates a major release of radioactive materials on par with the Chernobyl crisis. Government officials later said decommissioning the Fukushima Daiichi plant will take up to 40 years.

14 Military factions in Yemen clashed, killing one person. In Syria, protesters called for the release of detainees.

President Obama called for Congress to cut the nation's deficit by $4 trillion over 12 years by adopting a mix of revenue increases and spending cuts.

15 The FAA's top air-traffic-control official quit amid a controversy over controllers dozing on the job.

18 China stiffened banks' reserve requirements as Beijing battled inflation.

19 S&P lowered its outlook on U.S. government debt to "negative" from "stable," intensifying divisions over how best to tackle deficits.

20 Raul Castro was named leader of Cuba's ruling Communist Party.

21 The U.S. will scrap the color-coded terror-alert system and replace it with one designed to give the public more-specific information about "credible" threats. Later, the White House said in its first formal counterterrorism-strategy paper that Al Qaeda and its adherents remain the No. 1 security threat to the U.S.

23 Tens of thousands protested in Syrian cities. Security forces in several cities fired live ammunition and used tear gas to try to disperse the crowds, leaving at least 70 people dead, according to activists.

27 Sony said a hacker had obtained personal data for 77 million people who play online videogames through its PlayStation Network.

28 CIA Director Leon Panetta succeeded Robert Gates as defense secretary, while Afghan war commander David Petraeus took over as head of the spy agency.

Obama released his long-form birth certificate to prove he is a native-born citizen, in a bid to stop a fringe issue from moving mainstream.

Hamas and Fatah reached a power-sharing accord, ending a four-year rift between the Palestinian factions.

29 On this day, the Royal Wedding between Prince William and Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge went off with barely a hitch.

30 Syrian demonstrators defied a military crackdown. More than 50 people were killed, activists said, while an opposition group called on the military to take control in an attempt to bridge the gap between regime backers and protesters. The U.S. announced sanctions against senior Syrian officials, including members of the president's family.

MAY

1 Late on this day, Americans learned Osama bin Laden was killed during a raid by U.S. forces in Pakistan, where the al Qaeda leader was found living just 40 miles from the capital.

2 Federal officials assessed damage in the South from storms that brought flooding and tornadoes. More than 350 people were killed. Further deaths followed later in the spring, when storms struck the Midwest.

3 Silver prices tumbled 7.6% and gold dropped 1%.

5 Scientists ended a 52-year experiment that affirmed Einstein's theory of relativity.

6 Elvis left the list of the 1,000 most popular U.S. baby names for the first time since 1954.

10 S&P cut Greece's credit rating.

11 On this day, hedge-fund founder Raj Rajaratnam was convicted on all 14 counts of securities fraud and conspiracy. He later received a prison sentence of 11 years, the longest ever imposed in an insider-trading case.

Microsoft agreed to buy Skype for $8.5 billion, heading off a planned IPO by the Internet-communications firm.

12 Toyota's share of the global auto market slipped to third place as the company, formerly No. 1 in the industry, was hurt by a stronger yen and the March earthquake that hobbled plants in Japan.

14 On this day, Dominique Strauss-Kahn was arrested in New York on sexual-assault charges. Days later, he resigned as managing director of the International Monetary Fund. Prosecutors eventually gave up the case, saying the accuser's damaged credibility would have had a "devastating" effect at trial.

17 Google launched its first debt issue, $3 billion in bonds, as it joined other technology companies that have been cashing in on low interest rates to raise capital even as they sit on cash piles.

20 Obama pledged support for Arab uprisings and called for the first time to begin talks for a Palestinian state based on Israel's pre-1967 borders. Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the position, saying it would leave parts of Israel "indefensible."

LinkedIn's shares more than doubled to $94.25 in their opening day of trading.

24 California was ordered to reduce prison overcrowding. The decision grew out of lawsuits alleging treatment provided to mentally and physically ill inmates was so poor as to violate the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

25 In a speech to a joint session of the U.S. Congress, Israeli's Netanyahu rejected compromise on most of the issues at the heart of the Arab-Israeli dispute. He ruled out the division of Jerusalem, the return of Palestinian refugees or the withdrawal of all forces from the West Bank.

American International Group and the U.S. Treasury sold $8.7 billion in shares in a stock offering that garnered a small profit for taxpayers and began the government's exit from the insurer 2 1/2 years after its bailout.

26 UBS planned to separate its investment bank and incorporate it outside of Switzerland in an effort to placate regulators in that country who want to prevent another bailout should the financial giant fall on hard times.

27 The Supreme Court ruled constitutional an Arizona law requiring employers to verify workers' legal status and penalizing those that hire illegal immigrants.

31 Germany said it will close its nuclear reactors by 2022. The move will make Germany the first major economy to quit atomic energy since the nuclear crisis in Japan and marks a sharp policy reversal.

JUNE

1 Home prices in the U.S. were shown to have fallen to 2002 levels, effectively wiping out almost a decade's worth of home equity across the nation.

3 The USDA replaced its food-pyramid guideline with a food plate that emphasizes fruit and vegetables.

6 Yemen's youth opposition celebrated Ali Abdullah Saleh's departure. The president left for surgery in Saudi Arabia after he was wounded in a rocket attack, handing power to his vice president.

10 Newt Gingrich's presidential-campaign team quit following an internal debate over whether the former speaker was committed enough to the race.

13 The Dallas Mavericks won their first NBA title. Dirk Nowitzki was named MVP as the team took the crown with a 105-95 victory over the Miami Heat.

16 Pandora's shares rose 8.9% in their first session, down from an initial pop of 25%, amid a broader market selloff and questions about the firm's profit potential.

U.S. births fell in 2010 for a third-straight year, according to preliminary CDC figures.

The Boston Bruins won the NHL's Stanley Cup, beating the Vancouver Canucks 4-0 in Game 7.

17 Rep. Anthony Weiner resigned from Congress over an online scandal. The New York Democrat had admitted sending suggestive photos and holding lewd chats with women.

23 Obama ordered the withdrawal of 10,000 troops from Afghanistan this year, with remaining surge forces leaving by September 2012.

Alleged crime boss James "Whitey" Bulger, on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted List since 1999, was caught.

24 The U.S. and 27 other countries agreed to release 60 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves, temporarily driving down oil prices to a four-month low in a controversial bid to prop up the global economy.

25 A same-sex marriage law was approved by the New York state Senate. The first weddings under the law took place in July.

JULY

1 Hugo Chavez disclosed he has cancer. The Venezuelan president made the admission in a televised speech from Cuba, where he had surgery.

6 A scandal at News Corp.'s News of the World in the U.K. swelled with allegations of the possible hacking of a murdered teen's phone. The tabloid was later closed. And News Corp. founder Rupert Murdoch apologized to victims of phone hacking during a U.K. parliamentary hearing later in the month, but he deflected blame for the fiasco to other managers.

A jury acquitted Casey Anthony of killing her two-year-old daughter in a case that became a cable-TV sensation.

Portugal received a blow as Moody's downgraded its sovereign-debt rating to junk status.

7 A U.S. appeals court ordered an immediate halt to the ban on openly gay people serving in the military.

8 Died: Betty Ford, 93, former first lady.

9 On this day, South Sudan celebrated its first day in existence.

13 Moody's downgraded Ireland's bonds to junk status

14 Credit-rating firms warned of a potential downgrade of the U.S. government's debt if the federal borrowing limit isn't raised. Partisan wrangling over deficit cutting hit a new low as Obama ended a meeting with congressional leaders by declaring "enough is enough." Some GOP lawmakers want a balanced-budget amendment before voting to raise the government's borrowing limit. The drama continued through July.

18 Obama said he would nominate former Ohio Attorney General Richard Cordray to lead the new consumer finance watchdog agency. His nomination was held up through year's end.

Syrian forces moved on two border towns and arrested a leading writer after the opposition made a first attempt to form a shadow government.

21 On this day, space shuttle Atlantis returned to Earth, ending the final journey of a 30-year program.

22 Express Scripts entered a $29.1 billion deal to buy Medco Health Solutions.

23 Oslo was shaken by an attack from a far-right extremist. Anders Behring Breivik was accused of a bombing in a city center and a shooting spree at a youth camp that together killed at least 90 people.

27 McDonald's planned to fill its Happy Meal boxes with apple slices and smaller portions of French fries, the company's latest move to fend off more regulation of what kids eat.

AUGUST

1 Rep. Giffords, the Arizona Democrat who was critically wounded in a shooting in January, made her first appearance on the House floor to cast a yea vote for the debt bill. Her colleagues applauded her return. The Senate voted on the bill the next day, and Obama signed the bill to raise the nation's debt ceiling.

4 Japan intervened in currency markets to stem the rise of the yen against the dollar.

Egypt's ex-leader Mubarak pleaded not guilty as his landmark trial began on charges of killing protesters during the uprising earlier in the year.

5 The National Football League lockout officially ended when players approved a new collective-bargaining agreement.

6 S&P downgraded the U.S. government's triple-A credit rating, saying the recent budget deal didn't do enough to address the long-term picture for America's finances.

9 U.K. police struggled to contain rioting and looting across mostly poor and minority urban areas in the country's worst outbreak of social unrest in at least a decade.

12 Attorneys general in Virginia and Florida filed civil suits against Bank of New York Mellon alleging the bank cheated pension funds in those states by choosing improper prices for currency trades that it processed for the funds.

18 Nine weather disasters in 2011 have each caused more than $1 billion in damages, the National Weather Service says, tying a record.

22 Gadhafi lost his grip on Tripoli as Libyan rebels flooded the capital, encountering little resistance from the strongman's defenses.

26 Bank of America said it will get a $5 billion infusion from Warren Buffett, giving the banking giant a jolt of confidence as investors question its financial health.

27 Hurricane Irene menaced the Eastern seaboard, leaving dozens dead and millions without power. It largely spared New York after an unprecedented shutdown of the nation's biggest city.

31 On this day, solar-panel maker Solyndra announced plans to file for bankruptcy. The firm had received hundreds of millions in federal loan guarantees. Executives later pleaded the Fifth rather than testify about the company's collapse.

SEPTEMBER

3 A U.S. housing regulator filed lawsuits against 17 financial institutions, saying they sold $196 billion of risky home loans to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac without adequately disclosing risks.

6 Obama's approval ratings fell to their lowest level to date. A Wall Street Journal/NBC poll found 44% of Americans approved of his job as president; over half for the first time disapproved.

7 Yahoo's board ousted CEO Carol Bartz after growing impatient with the lack of a turnaround at the once-highflying Web firm.

Switzerland's central bank put a cap on the surging Swiss franc.

The 10-year Treasury yield finished below 2%.

8 A Soviet-era plane carrying members of a Russian pro hockey team crashed on takeoff, killing 43 people.

9 Obama proposed $447 billion in spending initiatives and tax cuts to boost economic growth in a speech to a joint session of Congress.

11 On this day, the U.S. marked the 10th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks largely without incident, but a truck bomb hit a military base in Afghanistan. The Taliban took responsibility for the blast, which it said was timed to mark the anniversary of 9/11. In New York, thousands of guests visited for the first time a monument that pierces Manhattan's bedrock where the World Trade Center towers formerly stood.

13 Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan announced a $5 billion cost-reduction plan that includes 30,000 job cuts as he fights to steady the lender and jump-start profits.

14 Median U.S. family income fell for the third-straight year to 1996 levels. The percentage of Americans living in poverty rose to 15.1%.

15 NASA unveiled plans for a $35 billion rocket program eventually powerful enough to launch astronauts to Mars, but big budget hurdles remain.

16 UBS alleged a rogue trader racked up as much as $2 billion in losses, marking the latest in a series of crises for the Swiss bank. The amount was later raised to $2.3 billion. Later, UBS Chief Executive Oswald Grubel resigned.

17 On this day, the first of what came to be known as the Occupy Wall Street protests got started in Manhattan's financial district.

22 Iran released two American hikers detained for more than two years after Iranian courts approved bail arrangements of $500,000 for each.

The Fed launched a new package of measures aimed at supporting a limping economy, deciding to dramatically recast its $2.65 trillion securities portfolio into longer-term U.S. debt through "Operation Twist."

23 Hewlett-Packard fired Leo Apotheker after 11 months as its chief executive and appointed former eBay chief Meg Whitman in his place.

European researchers said they clocked a particle exceeding the speed of light. Other physicists voiced skepticism.

24 Palestinians asked the U.N. to accept their plans for a member state in hopes of re-energizing a quest for an independent homeland, but the Security Council didn't take up the issue as support fell short of the nine votes required.

29 Amazon.com unveiled a new tablet, escalating its rivalry with Apple to provide both the devices and digital stores where people buy books, songs and movies.

30 McGraw-Hill and CME Group planned to combine stock-market icons such as the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 into a joint venture that would give the companies more sway over investors and exchanges.

Bank of America made plans to charge customers a monthly fee to use their debit cards. It -- and other big banks that were set to introduce such fees -- later canceled those plans amid customer and political backlash.

OCTOBER

1 One of the U.S.'s most-wanted terrorists, Anwar al-Awlaki, was killed in Yemen in what the U.S. said was a CIA drone strike.

4 An Italian appeals court acquitted American student Amanda Knox of murdering her roommate in 2007.

Sprint is making a multibillion-dollar gamble that access to Apple's iPhone will be the ticket to a turnaround for the wireless company.

5 On this day, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs died after a long battle with cancer. A day earlier, the company's new CEO, Tim Cook, stepped into the spotlight for the first time to unveil a new iPhone. Later in the month, Apple sold four million iPhone 4S smartphones in its first three days, the most for any iPhone launch.

8 Spain and Italy suffered debt downgrades, triggering a drop in the euro. Belgium was placed under review for a possible downgrade.

11 China's sovereign-wealth fund stepped in to buy shares of the country's battered banks, which have been caught in a selloff.

Netflix abandoned a plan to split its DVD-by-mail business from its online video-streaming service following a public backlash.

12 Israel and Hamas reached a deal to swap Gilad Shalit, an Israeli soldier jailed for more than five years in Gaza, in return for some 1,000 Palestinian prisoners.

13 Harrisburg, Pa., filed for bankruptcy protection.

14 Gap plans to shut more than a fifth of its Gap stores in North America over the next two years.

Galleon founder Raj Rajaratnam received a prison sentence of 11 years, the longest ever imposed in an insider-trading case.

15 Occupy Wall Street activists scored a victory when a cleanup of their encampment was canceled, as tensions escalated in other U.S. cities.

20 On this day, deposed Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi was shot and killed as Libyan forces overtook the city of his birth and last remaining stronghold, setting the stage for the nation to reinvent itself after a 42-year dictatorship.

21 The Basque separatist group ETA said it is laying down arms after over four decades of violence.

22 The yen surged to a record high against the dollar as traders questioned Japan's resolve to halt its rise.

24 Tunisia's election was the first in the region since citizens ousted ex-President Ben Ali and sparked revolts throughout the Mideast.

27 Rajat Gupta, a corporate director for such prominent firms as Goldman Sachs, was indicted on six criminal counts related to insider trading.

28 H-P said it will keep its personal-computer division, an about-face from its prior plan to explore splitting up the company.

On this day, the St. Louis Cardinals won baseball's Fall Classic, topping the Texas Rangers 6-2 in the seventh and deciding game of a back-and-forth series, capping off an unlikely run that included knocking off the Philadelphia Phillies and Milwaukee Brewers.

31 On this day, MF Global filed for bankruptcy protection after failing to reach a last-minute deal to sell itself. Later, the trustee overseeing the unwinding of the firm said more than $1.2 billion in customer funds could be missing.

NOVEMBER

1 The U.N. marked the birth of the world's seven billionth person. The population has more than doubled in 50 years.

3 Europe's leaders demanded that Greece declare whether it wanted to remain part of the euro zone after Greek Prime Minister Papandreou called a referendum on a bailout plan; the referendum was canceled.

4 Died: Andy Rooney, 92, "60 Minutes" curmudgeon.

5 Groupon closed at $26.11 in its first day of trading on the Nasdaq, up 31% from its IPO price of $20.

7 Died: Joe Frazier, 67, ex-heavyweight champ and rival to Muhammad Ali.

8 Michael Jackson's doctor was found guilty of involuntary manslaughter in the singer's 2009 death from an overdose of an anesthetic.

9 On this day, longtime Penn State football coach Joe Paterno was ousted by the college's board of trustees for failing to take stronger action following reports of alleged child sexual abuse by a former member of his coaching staff.

Japan's Olympus said it covered up investment losses for decades and used a series of acquisitions to clean up its books.

A federal appeals court rejected a challenge to the health-care overhaul, in a significant legal victory for the Obama administration.

The U.N. nuclear agency said Iran has developed technologies needed to make nuclear arms, the loudest alarm yet sounded by the IAEA.

16 New York police evicted Occupy Wall Street activists. In a predawn sweep, police cleared out a tent city in a downtown park.

22 Congress's deficit-cutting committee conceded defeat. Members were stymied by mistrust between Republicans and Democrats on the issues of taxes, Medicare and Social Security.

25 Yemen's president vowed to quit, but clashes grew as protesters denounced an immunity deal given Saleh and his circle.

29 A U.S. judge rejected a $285 million mortgage-bond pact with Citigroup. The ruling would affect enforcement efforts on Wall Street.

DECEMBER

1 Central banks moved to ease strains in financial markets through U.S. dollar loans to European banks, cheering investors in the U.S. and Europe.

Several European nations recalled envoys from Iran after Britain closed its embassy there and expelled Iranian diplomats from London, as the fallout from the raid on the U.K. Embassy in Tehran intensified.

5 Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin's party headed for a setback in Russia's parliamentary elections as Western observers said the election was neither free nor fair and was tipped in favor of Putin's United Russia just months before he seeks to return to the presidency. Protests took aim at Putin In the most direct challenge to Kremlin control since he came to power.

6 The Postal Service plans to end overnight delivery for basic letters in an effort to curtail billions in losses.

7 A top U.S. general urged a troop freeze in Afghanistan. Gen. John Allen, who commands U.S. and NATO forces in the country, is privately recommending staving off new U.S. troop reductions until 2014. A NATO assessment said quickly cutting troops would make it harder to clear and hold insurgent havens.

8 Some central banks in Europe have started weighing plans to prepare for the possibility that countries leave the euro zone or the currency union unravels entirely.

14 In a series of congressional hearings, former MF Global chief Jon Corzine defended his tenure but couldn't explain an estimated $1.2 billion in missing customer money.

15 More gloom descended on Europe as the euro sank below $1.30 and leaders underlined how far apart they remain on a way out of the region's crisis.

16 The U.S. military formally ended its mission in Iraq. The last of the 4,000 U.S. military personnel left over the course of the coming week, marking the end of the nearly nine-year war. The conflict resulted in tens of thousands of casualties -- including nearly 4,500 Americans dead -- and cost over $800 billion.

Social-game firm Zynga saw its IPO sour, in the biggest Internet debut since Google. Shares started up 10% but closed below their opening price at $9.45 each.

Global disasters this year caused a record $350 billion in damage, with less than a third covered by insurance, according to Swiss Re.

18 Died: Vaclav Havel, 75, Czech playwright and dissident who became president.

19 North Korean dictator Kim Jong Il died, opening a period of transition and instability for the region. Kim Jong Eun, the youngest of his three sons, will succeed him.

21 Astronomers discovered two Earth-size planets orbiting a Sun-like star in their search for habitable worlds.

22 Hundreds of euro-zone lenders took out $640 billion in low-interest loans from the European Central Bank, as the currency area extended a massive financial lifeline to its struggling banking industry.

25 The first day of NBA action as the lockout-delayed season began saw the defending champion Dallas Mavericks lose to the Miami Heat, 94-105.

28 Sears Holdings said that it will close as many as 120 stores.

30 The euro hit a 15-month low against the dollar as Europe's sovereign-debt woes continued to spook investors.

31 The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended up nearly 6% for the year, while the S&P 500 ended 2011 essentially flat and the Nasdaq fell. U.S. natural-gas prices fell to their lowest point in more than two years. Benchmark 10-year Treasurys ended under 2% for the first time since 1977. Gold retreated in the year's final weeks but still ended up 10%. Oil closed up on the year, trading right around $100 a barrel.
title: Year-End Review of Markets & Finance 2011 --- Protests, Crises and Celebrated Exits

text:
(WSJ Aug. 30, 2012)


(END)

TAMPA, Fla. -- A presidential election dominated by jobs, debt and the size of government has left little room for foreign policy, but that is set to change as Mitt Romney and the Republicans turn their sights on President Barack Obama's record overseas.

In a series of speeches starting with a Romney address Wednesday in Indianapolis, the Republicans will seek to portray the president as feckless and wavering in confronting threats in Syria, Iran, North Korea and China, Romney advisers said.

"In no region of the world is our influence stronger now than it was 3 1/2 years ago," said Alex Wong, Mr. Romney's top foreign-policy adviser.

The attacks carry some political peril, as they pit a GOP ticket lacking foreign-policy experience against a president who gets high marks from voters on that front.

GOP critics will also go after Mr. Obama for alleged leaks of classified information by his administration and for supporting cuts to military spending that could take effect next year if Congress fails to reach a budget agreement.

The critiques, including prominent speeches planned here at the GOP convention Wednesday by Sen. John McCain (R., Ariz.) and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, will mark a departure from a campaign largely focused on the country's economic woes.

Richard Haass, president of the nonpartisan Council on Foreign Relations, said Mr. Romney faces a difficult challenge trying to elevate foreign policy as a prime election issue when voters are focused on problems at home. "The question is whether he should avoid the issue or try to raise the decibel level," Mr. Haass said. "It appears he has decided to do the latter."

Mr. Romney and his running mate, Rep. Paul Ryan, have ground to make up on foreign policy. Voters give the president generally good grades for his global stance, with many noting the killing of Osama bin Laden, the administration's attacks against al Qaeda and the conclusion of the war in Iraq.

A Wall Street Journal/NBC News poll this month found 54% of voters approve of Mr. Obama's handling of foreign policy, his highest score in more than a year and far better than what either George W. Bush or Bill Clinton fetched as they sought re-election.

And for the first time in decades, the GOP ticket -- led by a former governor and a budget-focused congressman -- lacks strong overseas credentials. Mr. Romney has also been slow to elaborate on how his policies, particularly in confronting Iran or dealing with Afghanistan, would differ markedly from Mr. Obama's, critics say.

Meanwhile, two former Republican secretaries of state, James Baker III and Colin Powell, have praised Obama stances on China, Syria and Iran in recent months, with both pushing back against some of the more muscular statements coming from the Romney camp.

Romney foreign-policy aides say Republicans will use the limelight of the Tampa convention to lay out a wide-ranging critique of Obama policies, many of which were fleshed out in the party's own platform, which was released Monday.

The Romney camp for months has sought to portray Mr. Obama's policies as placing him outside of the bipartisan foreign-policy continuum stretching back to World War II. The campaign has been eager to draw parallels between Mr. Obama and President Jimmy Carter, whose presidency was overshadowed by the U.S. hostages in Iran and the failed attempt to rescue them.

"Romney is in the mainstream of U.S. foreign policy, while the outliers are Carter and Obama," said Rich Williamson, a former U.S. ambassador under President Ronald Reagan and a Romney foreign-policy adviser.

Mr. Romney and his advisers have leveled much of their strongest criticism at the administration's approach toward Syria and Iran. The U.S. has been far too timid, they say, in assisting the antigovernment opposition in Syria and too slow in ratcheting up pressure on Iran to stop its uranium-enrichment program. "In Syria, Obama has outsourced our diplomacy to the United Nations and given great leeway to Russia," said Mr. Wong, the Romney adviser.

Mr. McCain, a Vietnam War hero who lost to Mr. Obama in 2004, is expected to hit the president on the looming defense cuts, which both parties agreed to as part of a deal to raise the debt ceiling last year.

Even while pledging to cut the overall size of government, Mr. Romney wants to ramp up military spending by adding more troops and expanding the size of the navy, a plank that has stirred tensions within some portions of the party.

Democrats are quick to list Mr. Romney's foreign-policy mishaps. Earlier this year he called Russia the country's "No. 1 geopolitical foe," a remark that raised eyebrows even among some Republicans. His recent trip to Europe was overshadowed by several verbal stumbles.
title: Election 2012: Republicans Plan To Blast President On Foreign Policy

text:
His broad strokes offered a welcome contrast to Mr. Obama's view that America must defer to other nations to win global favor. Mr. Romney recognized the electorate's understandable war fatigue, but he still made a case for the world's only superpower to reassert its leadership, most of all in the Middle East.

A Romney Administration wouldn't "lead from behind" or defer to the United Nations. "If America does not lead, others will -- others who do not share our interests and our values -- and the world will grow darker, for our friends and for us," the candidate said.

Mr. Romney placed his criticism of the Administration's response to the attacks in Libya and elsewhere last month in this larger context. He stepped above the daily sniping over who knew what when and brought up the larger conflict. Contrary to the initial White House denials, Islamist terrorists burned down the consulate in Benghazi, killing the American Ambassador. This is part of a struggle started on 9/11 "between liberty and tyranny, justice and oppression, hope and despair," Mr. Romney said.

President Obama deserves credit for killing Osama bin Laden, but the Republican challenger is right to say that doesn't amount to a successful foreign policy. In the Middle East, as well as in Europe and Asia, current policy has been passive and ad hoc. Al Qaeda is far from dead, contrary to Obama spin. And the President's campaign pitch that the "tide of war is receding" is either naive or politically calculated, or both.

The boys in Chicago will keep saying that Mr. Obama has "strengthened our alliances and restored our standing." But come again? Ask Israel, Poland or Saudi Arabia how confident they are of America's friendship and resolve these days. The fires across the Middle East, from Libya to Syria to Iran, rage in a vacuum created by the perception that the U.S. is withdrawing from the region. Weakness emboldens adversaries, as Mr. Romney put it, whether Russia's Vladimir Putin, violent Arab Islamists or Iran's mullahs.

Mr. Romney's words were bolder than his proposals. He scored President Obama for abandoning the Syrians in their bloody 20-month struggle against Bashar al-Assad, who wasn't abandoned by his friends in Tehran and Moscow. The Turks and Saudis, who want to topple Assad, won't act without American buy-in.

Yet Mr. Romney promised only to work "through our international partners" to arm the Syrian opposition, which is not much more than the Obama Administration is doing. Mr. Romney might have called for direct American arms supplies or a possible no-fly zone or humanitarian corridors. He wants to avoid any suggestion of overseas adventures, but here was an opportunity to strike a substantive contrast with Mr. Obama.

On Iran, Mr. Romney recognized the aspirations of the country's people for self-determination and their hatred for a repressive theocratic regime -- in contrast to Mr. Obama's shameful refusal to support Iran's democratic movement in 2009.

On Iran's nuclear drive, Mr. Romney said he would boost the U.S. Navy presence in the Persian Gulf and strengthen economic sanctions, which Mr. Obama tried to water down in Congress before taking credit for them. But Mr. Romney notably did not repeat his July proposal that Iran must give up its demand to enrich uranium. The U.S. and Europe have wasted years looking for a diplomatic agreement to let the mullahs "enrich" peacefully. It'd be nice if the GOP candidate had taken this option off the table.

Mr. Obama and Vice President Biden have tried to use Mr. Romney's critique of their "run for the exits" strategy in Iraq and Afghanistan to portray him as a war monger. Among the better lines in the Romney speech was his rebuttal: "The route to war -- and to potential attacks here at home -- is a politically timed retreat that abandons the Afghan people to the same extremists who ravaged their country and used it to launch the attacks of 9/11." The details of his Afghan policy are vague, but count the disavowal of hasty drawdowns as an improvement.

In advocating a robust role for the U.S. overseas, Mr. Romney is placing himself in a long bipartisan tradition from Truman to Bush, while comparing Mr. Obama to Jimmy Carter in Presidential weakness. Foreign policy won't decide this election, but voters should be pleased that the Republican has forcefully made a case for renewed American leadership in the world.
title: Romney's World

text:
Mrs. Clinton long has said she would leave the job after one term. Now, however, in a sign of how much the tragedy has shaken her final days, she indicated in an interview that she may be willing to stay a bit longer.

"A lot of people have talked to me about staying," Mrs. Clinton said, declining to be more specific. When asked if current events will force her departure date to slip, she said it was "unlikely," but for the first time left open that possibility for the short term.

With presidential voting just days away, the suggestion she might stay could offer a sense of stability for Barack Obama as he makes his closing arguments. Mrs. Clinton has strong appeal among women voters as well, a possible swing constituency on Election Day.

Traveling with Mrs. Clinton in recent weeks, through New York, Asia and Washington, provides a close view of her role executing foreign policy for Mr. Obama, her onetime nemesis. In the Benghazi crisis, she made a previously undisclosed call to Libyan President Mohammed Magarief seeking immediate help in finding the missing U.S. ambassador, and later held a one-hour private meeting with him at the United Nations to urge him to disarm the militias and turn the tragedy into a "positive moment to propel Libya forward."

At the same time, she has faced rising violence in the Islamic world, a complex U.S. relationship with China and testy exchanges with Israel's prime minister over Iran's nuclear threat. These issues and others have gained prominence in the closing days of the U.S. presidential race. They also stand to shape Mrs. Clinton's legacy as secretary of state and her future political prospects.

As she rode to Andrews Air Force Base last month to meet President Obama for the arrival of the American bodies from Libya, Mrs. Clinton pressed the leader of one country where protests were still erupting outside the U.S. embassy. "Get your people there now," she said to him on the phone. "No excuses." Minutes later, she was out of the car, comforting the victims' families.

With President Obama occupied with re-election, Mrs. Clinton is doing much of the foreign-policy heavy lifting. And in the aftermath of the Libya attack that took the life of Ambassador Christopher Stevens, Mrs. Clinton put her own imprint on the debate by accepting blame. "I take responsibility," Mrs. Clinton said in an interview in her office.

As turbulence grew in recent weeks, the critiques of administration foreign policy have grown harsher. Much of the criticism was captured in this week's presidential debate, in which Republican Mitt Romney, while agreeing on some broad planks of the policy, was sharply critical of its execution.

He like others, charges that the administration has alienated allies, particularly Israel, raising the risk of military adventurism by enemies who think the U.S. won't stand up for its friends. He also charged that the Obama team has been tepid in supporting opposition forces trying to dislodge dictators, particularly in Iran and Syria, and has allowed Islamic extremists to step into the power vacuum created by the Arab Spring uprisings.

"I don't see our influence growing around the world," Mr. Romney charged. "I see our influence receding."

Some Republicans in Congress, though, have given Mrs. Clinton generally good reviews for taking blame for Benghazi and for her efforts to personally brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill as events there unfolded.

Rep. Darrell Issa, who held hearings this month skewering the administration, said in a statement, "Secretary Clinton showed leadership in acknowledging her ultimate responsibility for security failures," adding that "such a willingness to take responsibility in this administration has been too rare."

Whether President Obama wins or loses in two weeks' time, Mrs. Clinton is perceived as a 2016 White House contender both at home and abroad. The night of her arrival in Beijing last month, Chinese State Councilor Dai Bingguo told her over dinner, "You will be still be young when you are president."

Mrs. Clinton, 64 years old, says she laughed at his remark.

"I have ruled it out," Mrs. Clinton says of a presidential bid, in the living room of her State Department office. "It's important for me to step off this incredibly high wire I've been on," she says, "to take stock of the rest of my life."

Nevertheless, there is widespread assumption within the party that she can be persuaded to run. And in language that Democrats might perceive as an opening, Mrs. Clinton adds: "I will always want to be in service to my country."

One surprise of her tenure is her growing closeness to President Obama, four years after their intense battle in 2008's presidential race, aides to both say. When the bodies of the Americans slain in Benghazi were returned to Andrews Air Force Base, Mrs. Clinton held Mr. Obama's hand after his remarks. He put his arm around her waist when they left the podium.

"I know probably better than anyone. . .the difficult issues and hard questions he has to grapple with," says Mrs. Clinton, partly because of her years as first lady during Bill Clinton's presidency. Mr. Obama earlier this year gave Mrs. Clinton an iPad case inscribed with her initials. She gave him an espresso machine.

Even without the Benghazi crisis, Mrs. Clinton's final months figured to be frenetic. In recent weeks, she met with foreign leaders in eight countries, delivered 30 speeches, held 28 bilateral meetings and attended two dozen more events at the United Nations.

Through her years in the Senate, and now at the State Department, she also has engineered a shift in public opinions about herself, which were decidedly mixed during her husband's presidency. Mrs. Clinton's job-approval ratings, near 70% when most recently surveyed (prior to the Benghazi attack), compare favorably with her first lady years, when her approval rating bottomed out at 43% in Gallup polling after her failed attempt to overhaul health care.

One aspect of political life that she has been happy to ditch, her friends say, is "campaign mode" hair care, with blow-drys before appearances and other fussiness. Mrs. Clinton now wears her hair long, often pulled back. She considers it "more practical," says longtime friend Betsy Ebeling.

This fall, preparing for her final few months on the job, Mrs. Clinton set off for China. In her Air Force plane, which stocks fruit, almonds and Tabasco sauce, which she dribbles on nearly all foods, including salads, she slept on a foldout sofa in a private cabin. For meetings she sat in an armchair beside a garbage bag labeled "classified."

Just days prior, in Indonesia, Mrs. Clinton had urged China and its Southeast Asian neighbors to settle their territorial disputes in the oil-rich South China Sea collectively, "without coercion, without intimidation, without threats and certainly without the use of force." Those words irked Beijing.

About a half-hour after landing in China around 8 p.m., and wearing a trademark pantsuit, Mrs. Clinton emerged from her plane and went to meet with top Chinese brass. After handshakes for television cameras, both sides sat down for private meetings that stretched to 1 a.m.

The next morning, Mrs. Clinton brought U.S.-China tensions into the open. She and China's foreign minister, Yang Jiechi, held a news conference in the Great Hall of the People of China. Beforehand, Chinese aides steam-pressed the Chinese flags hanging behind the podiums.

Mrs. Clinton wasted no time tackling hot issues. After speaking pleasantly of "building habits of cooperation," she showed disagreement with her host not only on its territorial disputes in the South China Seas but also on its position to block U.N. action to end the violence in Syria.

Mr. Yang furiously took notes. As the translator relayed Mrs. Clinton's comments, he held up a finger to show he intended to respond.

Mrs. Clinton pressed on in the area of human rights, particularly in Syria, whose government is engaged in a bloody civil war where some 30,000 people have died. The U.S. is "disappointed," Mrs. Clinton said, in China's stance of using its veto power in the U.N. Security Council to, in effect, block sanctions against Syria. China's position is that Syria's crisis should be resolved through negotiations.

At Mrs. Clinton's next meeting, Premier Wen Jiabao scolded her, albeit in diplomacy-speak. "Our relationship was moving forward," he said. "But recently I'm more or less worried."

She describes her philosophy of the job as "public diplomacy" and talks about making a public case for what she calls the "American brand," saying, "We have to make the case for what we believe, for the right choices." With her China remarks, "I wanted my points to break through their mass media, and the international mass media," she says.

She returned to Washington and turned her attention to what she calls "economic statecraft," the effort to help American businesses abroad and at home. Deputy secretary Thomas Nides hosted travel-industry executives to highlight new visa standards for China and Brazil that increased visits from both places by 40% last year. "We live in an era where the size of our economy is just as important as the size of our army," Mrs. Clinton told them.

Then on Sept. 11, the State Department at 4 p.m. received an alert from its Libyan embassy in Tripoli. The U.S. ambassador, Mr. Stevens, visiting the Benghazi consulate, had delivered a one-sentence message: "We're under attack."

At 4:20 p.m., State Department executive secretary Steve Mull alerted Mrs. Clinton in her office. According to a person present, Mrs. Clinton asked, "How are we getting more security on the ground? More communication on the ground?"

And she said: "Find Chris," the U.S. ambassador. She had handpicked him for the posting.

At 5 p.m., Mr. Mull informed her that they couldn't locate the ambassador or reach his cellphone. But he said the department's "Ops Center" had an open line with the Tripoli embassy. Mrs. Clinton moved there for a video conference with White House, military and intelligence officials, who ordered increased security regionwide. Mrs. Clinton remained at the State Department until midnight.

Overnight, Mr. Stevens' body was identified at a Benghazi hospital. Mrs. Clinton returned to the State Department at 7 the next morning to inform the world of the tragedy.

She visited the bureaus within State where the slain Americans had worked and set up a video conference with their Libyan colleagues in Tripoli, who were visibly shaken. After recalling personal moments with Mr. Stevens, she told them, "Chris would want us to keep doing what he started."

American officials scrambled to understand the forces behind the attack. Initial intelligence indicated the violence was due to protests over an anti-Islamic video, made in the U.S. and spreading in the region at that time. Mrs. Clinton called the families of the four victims, consoled them and said the U.S. would bring the killers to justice.

The next three days, violent crowds continued at more than a dozen Muslim countries. In a single day in Islamabad, 19 people died. The State Department went on highest alert with the approach of Friday prayers, a day when demonstrations can grow as sermons are delivered.

Pakistan's government declared Friday, Sept. 21, a national holiday -- the Day of Love for the Prophet Muhammad -- in an attempt to calm the protests. Mrs. Clinton, however, worried the day off would have the opposite effect. She met with Pakistan's foreign minister to seek heavier security for the U.S. embassy. The Pakistani government went further, blocking cellphone signals in hopes of preventing coordinated riots.

Mrs. Clinton also worked on damage control at home, particularly with Congress. She went to Capitol Hill for all-member private sessions with senators and representatives.

The Obama administration has struggled to deliver a clear and consistent explanation of events the night of the Benghazi attack. Administration officials first called it the work of a spontaneous mob incited by the anti-Islam video then gaining prominence. Then it shifted its explanation to say the attack was the premeditated work of Islamic extremists.

At the same time, congressional hearings produced evidence that U.S. security officials in Libya had sought, but not received, stepped-up security to protect U.S. facilities in Libya and particularly in Benghazi.

Despite the political debate over when the administration determined the tragedy to be a terror attack, rather than the result of protests, Mrs. Clinton hasn't made that distinction within the State Department, one official says. "Once the compound was breached, no one here sat around deciding what to call it," this person says.

Since Benghazi, Mrs. Clinton is in constant touch with Mr. Obama and on the phone daily with his national security adviser, Tom Donilon, to review embassy security at "vulnerable" countries.

Even as the Benghazi crisis continued, another crisis bubbled up, this one involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over Iran's ambition to obtain nuclear weapons. Mr. Netanyahu was publicly criticizing the Obama administration for failing to set a "red line" that Iran wouldn't be allowed to cross in enriching uranium.

When the Sunday talk shows listed Mr. Netanyahu as a guest for Sept. 16, Mrs. Clinton decided she should privately reach out to him. Because Messrs. Netanyahu and Obama hadn't developed a close rapport, an administration official said, Mrs. Clinton wanted to call Mr. Netanyahu, whom she has known for decades.

In a 25-minute call Saturday, she set out to assure him, and temper his remarks the next day, by reinforcing the fact that the U.S. shared his goal of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The prime minister's office declined to comment.

"I've known Bibi a long time," Mrs. Clinton says, referring to Mr. Netanyahu. "I consider him a friend."

For now, Mrs. Clinton is putting off talk of her legacy, calling her job "all consuming." Recently she hit the road again, this time to Haiti with her husband for the opening of an industrial park. While there, Mr. Clinton reminisced about the couple's honeymoon on the island, 37 years ago.

Friends say the couple's power balance has become more equal during Mrs. Clinton's turn as secretary of state. Because the two keep busy schedules, it is often tough to find themselves in the same country, let alone the same city. Recently they celebrated their anniversary with an Indian dinner out. When together, the pair often talk about world problems and world leaders, friends say, and their desire for their daughter, Chelsea, to have a child.

In Haiti at the end of the day's events, the Clintons rode back to the airport together in the secretary of state's motorcade, which dropped off Mr. Clinton at his private plane. Then Mrs. Clinton's aircraft, the larger of the two, took off first.
